extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for assessing and formulating inductive inferences and accounts of causation in scientific and practical reasoning. Includes criteria distinguishing descriptions from explanations, conditions for valid induction, and pragmatic rules for naming causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity as condition of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition of the validity of every induction is that there be uniformity in the course of nature — not necessarily universal uniformity, but uniformity in the particular class of phenomena to which the induction relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is enough that uniformity pervades the class of phenomena concerned (e.g., planetary or magnetic phenomena) even if other phenomena (e.g., weather) are irregular. The induction implies either that the general fact of uniformity is already known, or that we are now entitled to infer it from the evidence (examples: conclusions about mortality from observed instances). Keeping this distinction dispels confusion about the grounds of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting explanations or predictions cannot both be true
rubrics_metrics.description: Different explanations of the same fact which posit incompatible mechanisms cannot both be true; likewise, conflicting predictions about a phenomenon cannot both be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Newtonian gravitation vs vortices (if one posits real vortices as the moving agency they exclude Newtonian mechanism); conflicting period predictions for a comet (300 years vs 400 years) — both cannot be right. Predictions that contradict each other show genuine incompatibility even if differing descriptions might coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between description and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'description' represents the facts or the manner of occurrence without asserting a mechanism; an 'explanation' attributes a cause or mechanism and may be true or false and may exclude other explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an earlier hypothesis (e.g., vortices) was merely a mode of representing motions, it could be reconciled with later theories; but if it posits a physical agent actively producing the effect, it is an explanation and may contradict another explanatory theory. Pay attention to whether a theorist is offering a representation (description) or asserting a mechanism (explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic rule for naming causes (informativeness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary discourse it is customary to name as the cause that condition which the hearer may require to be informed of — i.e., the informative or non-obvious antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: saying the surprise occurred because the sentinel was absent is acceptable if absence is the informative fact; one would say a person died for want of medical advice when that negative circumstance is what made the illness fatal. We do not normally name obvious or universally-expected conditions (possession of bodily organs) as causes unless they are the relevant informative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes are usually proximate antecedent events rather than antecedent states
rubrics_metrics.description: When people speak of causes they typically refer to proximate antecedent events (the immediate antecedent) rather than antecedent states or necessary background conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: we say the cause of a leap is not the muscles as a necessary condition; we say a book was written because the author had time (though 'having time' is a necessary condition, it's an antecedent state and not usually cited as the proximate cause). This helps distinguish which antecedents are appropriate to call 'cause' in explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative conditions may be called causes when they are the informative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative condition (the absence of something) can legitimately be spoken of as the cause if it is the condition that needs to be indicated and is what made the difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'died for want of medical advice' — the absence of advice is the cause spoken of; opening flood-gates as cause of flow (opening removes a negative restraint). The general formula of including negative conditions as absence of counteracting causes is not violated by such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law (or principle) of Composition of Causes and treatment of apparent exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes compose so that the collocation produced by causes combines; apparent exceptions (where duplicating a cause does not double the effect) arise when attention is paid to the remote rather than the immediate effect, or when a collocation threshold has been reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pointing two guns or exploding a second barrel at a different time/place doubles effect; two sparks may seem no more effectual than one for a single barrel because a single spark suffices to set off the explosive collocation. Double doses can produce larger or qualitatively different remote effects (aperients, laudanum). Evaluate whether an apparent non-additivity concerns immediate collocation or remote consequences; consider heteropathic laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive properties as apparent exceptions to causal composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties (e.g., opacity) seem purely preventive — manifesting only by defeating another agency — and may look like exceptions to causal composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases may be only apparent exceptions; the broader formula that views negative conditions as absence of counteracting causes still applies. Even if a property manifests only by blocking another effect, the practical application of causal rules usually remains intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical inferences can be inductive without explicit general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions drawn for the guidance of practical affairs often do not pass through expression as general propositions but can still exhibit intellectual rigor equal to scientific inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many practical inferences operate without stating a general law explicitly; Dr. Whewell's restriction of 'induction' to processes that produce general propositions is arbitrary according to the author. When evaluating practical reasoning, recognize inductive power even if no formal generalization is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior prejudices influence interpretation of experience but do not negate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Preconceived notions or a priori prejudices may predispose minds to certain interpretations of experience, but the erroneous opinions grounded in superstition nevertheless appeal to experience (coincidences) as their justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: belief that a comet presaged Caesar's assassination rested on appeals to observed coincidences. Recognize the role of antecedent presumption in making coincidences seem evidential, and separate suggestion of hypotheses from what evidence actually establishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of human actions from character (compatibilist test of causal claims about will)
rubrics_metrics.description: To assert that a person's actions necessarily follow from character means that the person invariably acts in conformity to that character, so that one who thoroughly knew the character could predict behavior — this is compatible with commonsense and does not entail metaphysical fatalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causal claims about volition, distinguish the claim 'actions follow from motives/character' (predictive, compatibilist) from stronger metaphysical claims of fatalism. The relevant test is predictability given full knowledge of character.
